issues.legal_issue: A claimant seeking beneficial ownership of property purchased in another person's name bears the initial burden of displacing the ostensible owner's title.
material_facts: The claimant asserted that several properties purchased in the other person's name had been acquired from funds generated by a business they carried on together.
The evidence did not establish that the business was joint or sufficiently profitable to fund the purchases, and no affirmative evidence traced the purchase money to joint funds.
The lower courts concurrently found that the claimant had not established joint ownership of the disputed properties.
issues.conclusion: The claimant did not prove that the properties were held benami or that he was their beneficial owner; the ostensible owner's title stood.
issues.legal_principle: The party asserting that property standing in another person's name is benami bears the initial onus of proving that assertion with cogent evidence, including evidence tracing the source of the purchase money to the alleged beneficial owner. The onus does not shift merely because the parties are brothers, own other property jointly, or the ostensible owner has not proved that he had sufficient personal funds. The amount and nature of evidence required depend on the circumstances.

predicates.claim_to_displace_ostensible_title: A claimant seeks to displace another person's apparent title by asserting that the property was acquired for the claimant's benefit.
predicates.property_purchased_in_another_persons_na: The property was purchased in the name of someone other than the claimant.
predicates.cogent_evidence_traces_purchase_funds_to: Convincing evidence traces the funds used to purchase the property to the claimant or to funds jointly belonging to the claimant and the named purchaser.

issues.definition: When a claimant challenges another person's apparent title to property purchased in that person's name and lacks convincing evidence tracing the purchase funds to the claimant, beneficial ownership is not established.

issues.legal_issue: A licensee cannot resist eviction on the ground that a licence is irrevocable when the defence was not pleaded or tried and the record does not establish the required permanent work.
material_facts: The owner sought possession of property from a person who was found to be occupying it as a licensee.
The occupant did not plead a defence that the licence was irrevocable, no issue on that defence was framed, and no evidence was led on it.
The occupant's counsel conceded that there was no finding that permanent work had been constructed on the property.
issues.conclusion: On the existing record, the occupant could not resist eviction by relying on Section 60 of the Indian Easements Act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 60 of the Indian Easements Act was invoked as the basis for an irrevocable licence. The Court held that the defence could not succeed on a record where it had not been pleaded, no issue had been framed, no evidence had been led, and no finding established permanent work. It considered Basratan v. Shiedattaraj distinguishable because the facts there were different.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding and irrevocable_licence_defence_not_pleaded and no_evidence_on_irrevocability and not permanent_work_established

predicates.eviction_proceeding: An owner seeks to evict a person occupying the owner's property as a licensee.
predicates.irrevocable_licence_defence_not_pleaded: The occupant does not plead that the licence is irrevocable.
predicates.no_evidence_on_irrevocability: No evidence is led to establish facts supporting the claimed irrevocability of the licence.
predicates.permanent_work_established: The record establishes that the licensee constructed permanent work on the property.

issues.definition: In an eviction proceeding, a licensee who did not plead or prove the basis for an irrevocable licence and whose record does not establish permanent work cannot resist eviction on that ground.

issues.legal_issue: A case should not be remanded for retrial without justification for reopening the proceedings.
material_facts: The case had been tried on evidence, and the lower courts had reached concurrent conclusions.
The appellant sought a remand, asserting that the other party's account was not entirely true and that a fresh inquiry would better serve justice.
The Court found no justification for reopening the case and sending it back for retrial.
issues.conclusion: The Court refused the request for remand and dismissed the appeals.
issues.legal_principle: The Court found no justification on the circumstances presented for reopening the case and ordering a retrial; it stated no separate statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this conclusion.

rule.if: appeal_seeking_remand and case_fully_tried and concurrent_lower_court_findings and not adequate_justification_for_reopening

predicates.appeal_seeking_remand: A party asks an appellate court to send the case back for a fresh trial or inquiry.
predicates.case_fully_tried: The case has already been tried on evidence.
predicates.concurrent_lower_court_findings: The lower courts reached the same conclusions on the case.
predicates.adequate_justification_for_reopening: The party seeking remand establishes a sufficient reason to reopen the case and conduct a fresh trial or inquiry.

issues.definition: When an appeal seeks remand after a case has been tried and the lower courts have reached concurrent findings, remand is refused if there is no adequate justification for reopening the case.
